what_a: Looks up an item's definition record from the game's item table by its id, returning a pointer to it or null when the id is negative or out of range.
what_b: Looks up an item definition by its numeric id, returning a pointer into the item table or null when the id is zero, negative, or out of range.
diff: For `id == 0` with a nonempty `items` array, A returns `&ctx.data.items[0]` while B returns `nullptr`. Negative and out-of-range ids return `nullptr` in both. A takes an `Item` and reads `item.id`, while B takes the raw `i32`, which is an argument-form change only.

what_a: Returns a copy of the input string with all ASCII uppercase letters converted to lowercase.
what_b: Returns a copy of the given string with all uppercase ASCII letters converted to lowercase, leaving other characters unchanged.
diff: Only for strings of 2^32 bytes (4,294,967,296) or longer. There, B's `u32 i` wraps around before reaching `r.size()`, so B loops forever while A returns the lowercased copy. For every shorter input, including embedded NULs, empty strings, and non-ASCII bytes, both produce identical results.

what_a: Parses a string of 1 or 2 ASCII digits into a non-negative integer, returning false if the text is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
what_b: Parses a string of digits into a 1-based party member number, returning 0 if the input is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
diff: Both accept only 1-2 digit strings and parse them the same way, but they report results differently. A returns bool and writes `out` only on success, so "0" and "00" give true with out=0 and any failure (non-digit, empty, too long) gives false with `out` untouched. B returns the value directly and uses 0 as its failure sentinel, so "0" and "00" return 0, indistinguishable from failure, and all failures also return 0. B's length limit is `kMaxMemberDigits`, which is not defined here, so B matches A only if that constant is 2; for a larger value, inputs of 3+ digits can be accepted by B and can overflow `i32`.

what_a: Parses a string of 1 or 2 ASCII digits into a non-negative integer, returning false if the text is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
what_b: Parses a string of up to six decimal digits into a non-negative integer without using exceptions, returning false if the string is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
diff: They differ only in the length cap. A rejects strings longer than 2 characters, while B accepts up to 6. So for any all-digit string of 3 to 6 characters (e.g. "100", "007", "123456"), A returns false and B returns true with the parsed value. Both reject empty strings and any non-digit character, and neither can overflow i32 within its limit.

what_a: Parses a text string into a 1-based party member number and returns false if the text isn't a number or falls outside the valid party size range.
what_b: Parses a text string into a 1-based companion slot number, returning false if the text isn't a number or falls outside 1 to kCompanionSlots.
diff: The two functions differ only in the upper bound: companionsParseMember accepts 1..kPartyMaxSize, while companionsParseSlot accepts 1..kCompanionSlots. Inputs whose parsed number n satisfies n > min(kPartyMaxSize, kCompanionSlots) but n <= max of the two give different results. For example, if kPartyMaxSize = 6 and kCompanionSlots = 4, then "5" is accepted by companionsParseMember but rejected by companionsParseSlot. Results are identical when the two constants are equal, and the lower bound (n < 1) and the parse step are identical in both.

what_a: Looks up the display name of a quest guild from a name table by its enum index, returning an empty string if the index is out of range.
what_b: Looks up the display name for a guild by converting the Guild enum value to an integer index into a name table and returning that string.
diff: For out-of-range guild values (idx < 0 or idx >= kGuildCount), A returns an empty Str while B indexes kGuildNames out of bounds, which is undefined behaviour. For in-range values, A reads kQuestGuildNames and B reads kGuildNames, so they differ wherever those tables disagree at the same index, which I cannot verify from these snippets.

what_a: Returns the string value stored under a given key in the session's feature-state map, or an empty string if the key is absent.
what_b: Looks up a string value by key in the session's feature-state map and returns it, or a supplied default if the key is absent.
diff: When `key` is present in `s.featureState`, both return the stored value. When `key` is absent, A returns an empty `Str`, while B returns `dflt`. The two only agree on absent keys when `dflt` is empty. A is B with `dflt = Str()`, so A can be replaced by B with an added argument, but B cannot be replaced by A at call sites that pass a non-empty default.

what_a: Returns a reference to the square at grid coordinates (x, y) in the floor's square array, by converting the coordinates to a cell index.
what_b: Returns a read-only reference to the square at grid coordinates (x, y) in the floor's square array, converting the coordinates to a flat index via cellOf.
diff: Both index `floor.squares` with the same `cellOf(x, y)`, so they return the same square for the same coordinates. They differ in constness: A takes a non-const `FloorState&` and returns a mutable `SquareState&`, so it works for writes. B takes a `const FloorState&` and returns `const SquareState&`, so it accepts const floors but its result cannot be modified. A call site that writes through the result of a non-const floor fails to compile if switched to B. A call site with a const floor fails to compile with A.

what_a: Parses a string of up to six decimal digits into a non-negative integer without using exceptions, returning false if the string is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
what_b: Parses a string of digits into a 1-based party member number, returning 0 if the input is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
diff: For any valid all-digit input of 1 to 6 characters, both return the same value (e.g. "42" gives 42 in both). They differ in failure signalling: A returns false and leaves `out` untouched on bad input, while B returns 0. So for "0" A reports success with value 0, but B returns 0 with no way to tell it apart from an error. For invalid input such as "", "x1", "1234567" or "-5", A returns false and B returns 0. If kMaxMemberDigits is not 6, the accepted lengths also differ, but that constant's value isn't shown.

what_a: Converts 1-based (x, y) grid coordinates into an index in the flat square array of a floor, returning a pointer to that square or nullptr if the coordinates or index fall outside the map.
what_b: Returns a pointer to the square at 1-based coordinates (x, y) in a floor's row-major square array, or nullptr if the coordinates fall outside the 30-wide map or past the end of the stored squares.
diff: Results differ whenever kMapWidth != kViewMapWidth (for example, (x=1, y=2) maps to index kMapWidth in A and kViewMapWidth in B), and B returns a const pointer to a const floor while A returns a mutable pointer to a non-const floor, so call sites that write through the result cannot switch to B. If the two constants are equal (the comment in B says 30), the index math and bounds checks are identical for all inputs.

what_a: Rounds a double to four decimal places using half-even rounding and returns it as a 64-bit fixed-point integer, with no game meaning of its own.
what_b: Rounds a double to the nearest integer using round-half-to-even (banker's rounding) and returns it as an i64, with no game meaning of its own.
diff: Read literally, B(x) and A(x) differ for every nonzero input because A scales by 10000 first. Examples: x=0.5 gives A=5000 and B=0; x=1.0 gives A=10000 and B=1; x=2.5 gives A=25000 and B=2; x=-2.5 gives A=-25000 and B=-2. Assuming `roundHalfEven` implements the same half-even rule as B (its body isn't shown), A(x) equals B(x*10000.0) for all x, so the only difference is the scaling, which is an argument-form change. B's floor-based logic is correct for negative values and exact tie-breaking, so the two agree on rule and on their own domain.

what_a: Parses a string of decimal digits with an optional leading minus sign into a 32-bit integer, returning false if the text is malformed or the magnitude exceeds 1,000,000,000.
what_b: Parses a string of decimal digits into a 32-bit integer, rejecting empty input, non-digit characters, and values above 1,000,000.
diff: A accepts a leading '-' and returns the negative value (e.g. "-5" gives -5, "-0" gives 0), while B rejects any '-'. A's upper bound is 1000000000 and B's is 1000000, so inputs such as "1000001" through "1000000000" succeed in A and fail in B. Both accept unsigned inputs up to 1000000 with identical results, and both reject empty strings, "-" alone, "+5", and non-digit characters.

what_a: Parses a non-negative decimal integer from a string without throwing exceptions, returning false for empty, non-numeric, or out-of-range (above 1,000,000) input.
what_b: Parses a string of decimal digits into a 32-bit integer, rejecting empty input, non-digit characters, and values above 1,000,000.
diff: Both accept plain digit strings in 0..1000000 and reject empty, non-digit, and out-of-range input. Their results can differ for inputs that depend on `accParseInt`, whose source isn't provided. If `accParseInt` accepts a leading sign, A returns true for "+5" and for "-0" (out=0), while B rejects both. If `accParseInt` doesn't guard against i64 overflow, A can wrap on very long digit strings and accept some values B rejects, while B stops as soon as the running value passes 1000000. Whitespace handling is also unknown without `accParseInt`'s source.

what_a: Parses a string of 1 or 2 ASCII digits into a non-negative integer, returning false if the text is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
what_b: Parses a string of 1 to 4 digits into a non-negative integer, returning false if any character is not a decimal digit.
diff: Both functions accept only non-empty all-digit strings, and they return the same value for every input of length 1 or 2. They differ for all-digit strings of length 3 or 4 (e.g. "100", "999", "0042", "9999"): Function A returns false, while Function B returns true and sets out to the parsed value.

what_a: Returns a lower-case ASCII copy of a string by shifting A–Z to a–z, leaving all other characters unchanged.
what_b: Returns a copy of the given string with all uppercase ASCII letters converted to lowercase, leaving other characters unchanged.
diff: Only for strings of 2^32 bytes (4 GiB) or more. There, B's `u32` index wraps and the loop never terminates, while A returns the lowered copy. For all shorter inputs both map exactly 'A'-'Z' to 'a'-'z' and leave every other byte unchanged.

what_a: Compares two strings for equality ignoring case, returning true when the typed word matches the given name.
what_b: Compares two strings for equality ignoring trailing spaces and letter case, a generic text helper that the roster name matching uses.
diff: Trailing spaces. Function B ignores them and Function A does not, so sameName(A)("abc ", "abc") is false but sameName(B)("abc ", "abc") is true, and likewise for trailing spaces on the name argument. Both are case-insensitive and otherwise agree, including for leading spaces. Their case folding may differ for non-ASCII bytes if lowerCopy is not ASCII-based, and I could not see lowerCopy's definition to rule that out.

what_a: Subtracts a given number of years from a character's age (in days) for effects like the Potion of Youth or Dragon's Blood, flooring the result at zero so age can't go negative.
what_b: Ages the character by the given number of days, clamping the result at zero so that negative aging effects like the Potion of Youth or Dragon's Blood cannot make a character younger than newborn, and announces the new age to the player.
diff: The resulting `ageDays` matches for every input when B is called with `days = -years * kDuseYearDays`, including the clamp to 0. B also calls `ctx.say("progression.age", ...)` on every call, which A never does, so replacing A with B changes output at every call site. Call sites also need a different argument form (`years` vs. signed `days`) and a `Ctx&` argument.

what_a: Returns a reference to the square at grid coordinates (x, y) in the floor's square array, by converting the coordinates to a cell index.
what_b: Converts 1-based (x, y) grid coordinates into an index in the flat square array of a floor, returning a pointer to that square or nullptr if the coordinates or index fall outside the map.
diff: For in-range inputs (1 ≤ x ≤ kMapWidth, 1 ≤ y, index within the array) both return the same square, assuming `cellOf` uses the same 1-based row-major formula. They differ for x < 1 or y < 1 (A computes an index that may be out of bounds or wrap, B returns nullptr), for x > kMapWidth (A silently returns a square in the next row, B returns nullptr), and for any index past the array end (A is undefined behaviour, B returns nullptr). A returns a reference and B returns a pointer, so call sites also need `&`/`*` and null checks, which is more than an argument-form change.

what_a: Parses a string of up to six decimal digits into a non-negative integer without using exceptions, returning false if the string is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
what_b: Parses a string of 1 to 4 digits into a non-negative integer, returning false if any character is not a decimal digit.
diff: A accepts digit strings of length 5 or 6 (e.g. "12345" -> 12345, "999999" -> 999999, "00001" -> 1), but B returns false for them. B accepts length 1 to 4 only, so "12345" and "00001" are rejected. Both accept lengths 1 to 4 with identical values, and both reject empty strings and any non-digit character.

what_a: Returns the string value stored under a given key in the session's feature-state map, or an empty string if the key is absent.
what_b: Looks up a string value by key in the session's featureState map for the seer's pending person offer, returning an empty string if the key is absent.
diff: (1) A `nullptr` key is possible for B but not A. Constructing a `Str` from a null `const char*` is undefined behaviour (typically a crash or exception), while A cannot receive a null key. (2) A `Str` key containing an embedded `'\0'` behaves differently when passed through B's `const char*` parameter, because the conversion truncates at the NUL. A looks up the full key, while B looks up only the prefix before the NUL, so the two can return different values. Both assume `featureState` is keyed by `Str` (for example `std::map<Str, Str>`).

what_a: Parses a decimal integer string (with optional leading minus sign) into a 64-bit value, setting an ok flag to false if any character is not a digit.
what_b: Parses a string into a signed 64-bit integer, accepting an optional leading minus sign and rejecting non-digit characters or values above 10^12.
diff: Both accept an optional leading '-' followed by one or more ASCII digits, and both reject "", "-", "+5", and any non-digit. They differ for inputs whose magnitude exceeds 1000000000000: B rejects them (e.g. "1000000000001"), while A accepts them and overflows i64 (undefined behaviour) for very long inputs. On failure, A sets ok=false and returns 0, while B returns false and leaves `out` unchanged, so a caller that reads the value after a failed parse sees different results.

what_a: Returns the height of a floor map by dividing its total field count by the floor's own width, or 0 if the width is non-positive.
what_b: Returns the number of rows in a floor's square grid by dividing the total square count by the map width.
diff: Results differ whenever `def.width` (A) is not equal to `kMapWidth` (B), since A divides by the floor's own width and B by the global constant. For example, with 100 fields and a floor width of 10 versus `kMapWidth` of 20, A returns 10 and B returns 5. A returns 0 when `def.width <= 0`, while B has no guard and would divide by zero if `kMapWidth` were 0. Also, B's argument is a `FloorState` with a `squares` member and A's is a `FloorDef` with a `fields` member, so call sites need argument changes, and the two containers are only interchangeable if they hold the same cells.

what_a: Computes the experience points a character needs to reach a given level, summing per-level thresholds from the guild and race experience factors and then applying the race experience multiplier.
what_b: Computes the threshold experience points needed for a character at level x, scaled by the guild's experience factor and the race's experience multiplier, rounded to a whole number (returns 0 for x ≤ 0).
diff: Both return 0 for level/x <= 0, but for positive inputs they differ. B omits the engine's constant term (-0.264, per its own UNKNOWN comment) and its closed form lacks A's "-2" offset inside the /10 bracket, so B's results are off by a constant-like amount at every positive level. A applies curFixed truncation at each intermediate step, while B works in plain double and rounds only at the end. A takes raw doubles (guildExp, raceExp) and computes the race multiplier from raceExp+1, while B takes Guild/Race enums and looks up kGuildExpFactor and kRaceExpMult, so call sites need argument conversion as well as the result differences.

what_a: Returns a read-only reference to the square at grid coordinates (x, y) in the floor's square array, converting the coordinates to a flat index via cellOf.
what_b: Converts 1-based (x, y) grid coordinates into an index in the flat square array of a floor, returning a pointer to that square or nullptr if the coordinates or index fall outside the map.
diff: Inputs outside the map give different results. For x < 1, y < 1, x > kMapWidth, or y beyond the last row, B returns nullptr while A indexes with whatever cellOf returns, which is undefined behaviour if the index is out of range and may silently return a square from a neighbouring row when x wraps. A returns a const reference and B a nullable mutable pointer, so call sites that test for nullptr would break if A replaced B.

what_a: Returns a reference to the party member at the given index, converting the signed index to unsigned to access the members container directly, with no game rule applied.
what_b: Returns a read-only reference to the party member at index i, converting the signed index to unsigned for the members array lookup without any game rule applied.
diff: For every input (party and index), both return the same element, and reads agree. They differ only in constness: A returns `Character&` and B returns `const Character&`, so a write through A's result (e.g. `memberAt(p, 0).hp -= 5`) does not compile with B. A also rejects a `const Party&` argument, which B accepts.

what_a: Parses a decimal integer string (with optional leading minus sign) into a 64-bit value, setting an ok flag to false if any character is not a digit.
what_b: Parses a decimal integer from text, accepting an optional leading minus sign and stopping at the first non-digit, returning 0 for unreadable input.
diff: For any input with a non-digit after an optional leading '-' that is preceded by at least one digit, A returns 0 and B returns the leading digits: "12abc" (A=0, B=12), "3.7" (A=0, B=3), "-12x" (A=0, B=-12), "5 " (A=0, B=5). A also sets ok=false for these, while B has no ok output at all. Inputs that are entirely digits (with optional '-'), or that have no leading digits such as "", "-", "abc", "+5", and "-x", give the same result in both (0, or the signed value).

what_a: Looks up a string value by key in the session's feature-state map and returns it, or a supplied default if the key is absent.
what_b: Looks up a string value by key in the session's featureState map for the seer's pending person offer, returning an empty string if the key is absent.
diff: When `key` is present, both return the stored value and the results match. When `key` is absent, A returns `dflt` and B returns an empty `Str()`, so they differ whenever `dflt` is non-empty (e.g., `storedOr(s, "k", "x")` yields `"x"` but `seerGet(s, "k")` yields `""`). A can replace B by passing `""` as the third argument; B cannot replace A at call sites that pass a non-empty default.

what_a: Resolves a player's typed guild argument, either a numeric index or a guild name compared case-insensitively, to a valid guild index for the guild log command, returning false if no valid guild matches.
what_b: Parses a typed word as either a numeric index or a case-insensitive name into a Guild enum value, returning false if neither matches a valid guild.
diff: (1) Surrounding whitespace: " 2", "Warrior " and similar inputs are trimmed by A but not by B, so A accepts them and B rejects them (unless parseNum/lowered happen to strip whitespace, which the shown code does not indicate). (2) Upper-case names: A lowercases both the input and each stored name, so "WARRIOR" matches under A; B lowercases only the input and compares it to kGuildNames, so it matches only if those constants are already lowercase. (3) Valid index range: A bounds-checks against the session's glGuildCount(s), while B bounds-checks against the constant kGuildCount, so an index in [session count, kGuildCount) is accepted by B and rejected by A if the two counts differ. (4) Name source: A reads names via glGuildName(s, i), B reads kGuildNames, so any mismatch between those sources changes results. (5) Numeric parsing: glParseInt on the trimmed, lowercased string and parseNum on the raw string may disagree on forms such as "+3" or "0x2"; I could not verify this since neither helper is shown.

what_a: Looks up the display name for a guild by converting the Guild enum value to an integer index into a name table and returning that string.
what_b: Maps a Guild enum value to its display name string, returning "?" for any unrecognized value.
diff: For every valid `Guild` value, the two functions agree only if `kGuildNames[i]` holds the same string as the literal in B's matching case. That table isn't visible here, so this can't be confirmed. For an out-of-range enum value, A indexes past the array (undefined behaviour), while B returns `"?"`.

what_a: Reports whether a monster group in the current encounter is still standing, meaning it has at least one living member, and returns false for any out-of-range group index.
what_b: Reports whether a monster group still has at least one living member, which the game's melee rules (R2, R3, R5) use to decide if the group keeps fighting.
diff: For any in-range index, groupStanding(game, g) equals groupStanding(game.encounter.groups[g]). The exception is an out-of-range index (g < 0 or g >= kMaxGroups): Function A returns false, while Function B has no index to receive and would need a call site that indexes first, which is undefined behaviour for such g.

what_a: Parses a party member number from the second word of a typed command and checks that it falls within the current party size, returning whether it is valid.
what_b: Parses a 1-based party member number typed as a string, checks it falls within the party size, and converts it to a 0-based index.
diff: For any valid input such as "3" with party size 4, A sets member=3 (1-based) and B sets idx=2 (0-based). A returns false when w.size()<2 and takes its input as a word list, while B takes a single string. Both reject values outside 1..party size, but A bounds with accPartySize(s) and B with s.game.party.size, which are equal only if accPartySize returns that field.

what_a: Returns the first pack slot (slots 2 through kPackSlots, skipping the Hands slot) of a party member that holds no item, or nullptr if the pack is full.
what_b: Scans the pack inventory from slot 1 upward (skipping the Hands slot at 0) and returns the index of the first slot whose item id is 0, or -1 if the pack is full.
diff: (1) Empty test: A treats any item with id <= 0 as free, so a slot holding a negative id is free in A but occupied in B (B requires id == 0). (2) Return convention: A returns an Item* or nullptr, while B returns an internal index or -1, so call sites must change even though the argument form can match. (3) Argument form: A takes Session& and a 1-based member, while B takes const Inventory&. Assuming accPackItem's 1-based slot k maps to internal index k-1, both scan the same pack range (indices 1..kPackSlots-1) with Hands excluded.

what_a: Parses a text string into a 1-based party member number and returns false if the text isn't a number or falls outside the valid party size range.
what_b: Parses a 1-based party member number typed as a string, checks it falls within the party size, and converts it to a 0-based index.
diff: (1) Output value: for every accepted input k, A sets member1 = k while B sets idx = k-1 (e.g. "1" gives member1 = 1 in A and idx = 0 in B). (2) Upper bound: A accepts up to the constant kPartyMaxSize, while B accepts only up to s.game.party.size, so with a party of 2, "3" returns true in A (member1 = 3) and false in B. (3) The underlying parsers differ (companionsParseNumber into i32 vs. parseNum into i64), and their handling of malformed or overflowing text is not shown, so those inputs may also differ.

what_a: Formats a gold amount stored in 1/10000 gold units as a decimal string with a " gold" suffix, omitting the fractional part when it is zero.
what_b: Formats a signed 1/10000-gold currency amount as a decimal gold string with a minus sign for negatives and four fractional digits zero-padded.
diff: (1) A appends " gold" to every result and B never does, so results differ for every input (e.g. 15000 gives "1.5000" from B and "1.5000 gold" from A; the frac-is-nonzero case also differs by that suffix alone). (2) Zero fraction: units=50000 gives "5.0000" from B and "5 gold" from A, since A omits the decimal point and B always keeps it. (3) Negatives: units=-5 gives "-0.0005" from B, but A computes whole=0 and frac=-5, so it emits non-digit characters (e.g. '+') in the output. (4) Units with a nonzero fraction are otherwise formatted identically (4-digit zero-padded fraction, e.g. 10 gives "0.0010" in B and "0.0010 gold" in A).

what_a: Converts a 1-based (x, y) map coordinate into a single linear square index by row-major arithmetic on the map width.
what_b: Converts a 2D map coordinate (x, y) into a flat array index by row-major order using the map's side length.
diff: For every (x, y), A(x, y) = x + 30(y−1) and B(x, y) = x + kMapSide·y. If kMapSide = 30 (not confirmed; the constant is not in the excerpts), B(x, y) − A(x, y) = 30 for all inputs, so results differ everywhere. For any other kMapSide, the gap is y·(kMapSide − 30) + 30, which also varies with y. Example: A(1,1) = 1, while B(1,1) = 31 if kMapSide = 30.

what_a: Formats a signed integer amount of 1/10000ths of a gold piece as a plain decimal string with trailing zeros removed, like "-12.25" or "3".
what_b: Formats a signed 1/10000-gold amount as a human-readable string with up to four decimal places and trailing zeros removed, followed by " gold".
diff: For every input, storeGoldText appends " gold" and hallCurrencyText does not (e.g. v=2500: "0.25" vs "0.25 gold"; v=120000: "12" vs "12 gold"; v=0: "0" vs "0 gold"; v=-5000: "-0.5" vs "-0.5 gold"). The numeric part is identical, assuming Currency is an integral type that behaves like i64 and toStr matches std::to_string.

what_a: Counts how many monsters in the current encounter are still alive, which the combat round logic uses to decide whether the fight continues.
what_b: Counts how many monsters in the encounter still have hit points above zero, so the combat logic can tell how many foes are left standing.
diff: They disagree when a monster's `alive` flag and its `hits` field conflict. A counts a monster with `alive == true` and `hits == 0` (B does not). B counts a monster with `alive == false` and `hits > 0` (A does not). They agree on any monster where `alive` and `hits > 0` match.

what_a: Parses a string of digits into a non-negative integer, rejecting empty strings, signs, non-digit characters, and values above 100000.
what_b: Parses a string of decimal digits into a 32-bit integer, rejecting empty input, non-digit characters, and values above 1,000,000.
diff: Both reject empty strings and any non-digit character (including signs and whitespace). They differ only in the upper bound. A rejects any value above 100000, so "100001" through "1000000" return false. B accepts them and sets `out` to the value, so "100001" gives out=100001 and "1000000" gives out=1000000. Values from 0 to 100000 are accepted by both, and values above 1000000 are rejected by both.

what_a: Returns the trimmed name of the guild at a given index, or the index as text if the index is out of range.
what_b: Looks up the display name of a quest guild from a name table by its enum index, returning an empty string if the index is out of range.
diff: (1) Out-of-range guild index: A returns the number as text (e.g. -1 gives "-1", and 7 gives "7" if there are 7 guilds), while B returns an empty string. (2) In-range names: A returns the session's stored name with glTrim applied, while B returns the untrimmed kQuestGuildNames entry, so names with surrounding whitespace differ. (3) Name source and bounds: A reads s.data.guilds with bound glGuildCount(s), while B reads a compile-time table with bound kGuildCount, so they can disagree if session data has different names or a different count.

what_a: Parses a non-negative decimal integer from a string without throwing exceptions, returning false for empty, non-numeric, or out-of-range (above 1,000,000) input.
what_b: Parses a string of decimal digits with an optional leading minus sign into a 32-bit integer, returning false if the text is malformed or the magnitude exceeds 1,000,000,000.
diff: (1) Negative input: "-5" gives false from A (non-digit) but true with out = -5 from B. (2) Range: "1000001" gives false from A (above 1000000) but true with out = 1000001 from B; B accepts up to 1000000000, and -1000000000 down. (3) Overflow: B's bound check runs after `v*10 + digit`, so long inputs such as "9999999999" overflow the i32 before the check, which is undefined behaviour; A is not affected by this. (4) Leading '+', whitespace, or other characters depend on `accParseInt`, which is not shown, so they may differ.

what_a: Parses a string of digits into a 1-based party member number, returning 0 if the input is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
what_b: Parses a string of 1 to 4 digits into a non-negative integer, returning false if any character is not a decimal digit.
diff: (1) Input "0": A returns 0, which is also its failure value, so the caller cannot tell "0" from rejection; B returns true with out=0. (2) Inputs of 5 to kMaxMemberDigits digits (e.g. "12345"): A parses them, while B returns false because its limit is 4. This is a difference only if kMaxMemberDigits > 4, and that constant's value is not shown. (3) If kMaxMemberDigits ≥ 10, A can overflow i32 (undefined behaviour) on long digit strings, while B cannot, since its 4-digit limit prevents overflow.

what_a: Parses a string of digits into a non-negative integer, rejecting empty strings, signs, non-digit characters, and values above 100000.
what_b: Parses a string of 1 to 4 digits into a non-negative integer, returning false if any character is not a decimal digit.
diff: A accepts values up to 100000 at any digit length, so "10000" through "100000" and any zero-padded form like "00001" (length 5 or more) are accepted by A and rejected by B. B rejects anything longer than 4 characters, so "12345", "99999", and "00001" give true in A and false in B. Both accept "0"–"9999" with 4 or fewer characters, and both reject empty strings, signs, non-digits, and values above 100000 (e.g., "100001").

what_a: Looks up the display name of a quest guild from a name table by its enum index, returning an empty string if the index is out of range.
what_b: Maps a Guild enum value to its display name string, returning "?" for any unrecognized value.
diff: For out-of-range values (negative, or at least kGuildCount, or any non-enumerator value cast to Guild), A returns an empty string and B returns "?". For valid guilds, they agree only if kQuestGuildNames has the same strings as B's literals, in the same order as the Guild enum; the table isn't visible, so this is unverified, and a mismatch would be an additional difference.

what_a: Compares two strings for equality ignoring case, returning true when the typed word matches the given name.
what_b: Compares two strings for exact equality by checking that their lengths match and that one starts with the other.
diff: Strings that differ only in letter case, e.g. ("Gold", "gold") or ("Abc", "aBC"): sameName/A returns true, seerSameText/B returns false (assuming seerStartsWith is a plain case-sensitive prefix test). Equal-length strings that differ in other ways agree (both false), and empty-vs-empty agrees (both true).

what_a: Returns the name string at index i from a fixed-size array of names, or an empty string if the index is out of range.
what_b: Looks up the display name of a quest guild from a name table by its enum index, returning an empty string if the index is out of range.
diff: Both return the name at a valid index and an empty `Str` otherwise, but they validate against different bounds. A uses the array extent `N`, while B uses `kGuildCount`. If `kGuildCount` equals `N`, the results match for every index. If `kGuildCount` is smaller than `N`, B returns empty for indices in `[kGuildCount, N)` where A returns a name. If `kGuildCount` is larger than `N`, B reads past the end of `kQuestGuildNames` (undefined behaviour) for indices in `[N, kGuildCount)` where A returns empty. B also takes a `Guild` enum rather than an `int`, so call sites would need an argument change.

what_a: Searches a list of floor states for the one whose dungeon level matches the given level and returns its index, or -1 if none matches.
what_b: Linear search over the game's floor list that returns a pointer to the floor whose dungeon level matches the given level, or null if none does.
diff: Both find the first floor whose dungeonLevel equals `level`, but the results differ in form: A returns the index (i32) or -1 when absent, while B returns a `FloorState*` or `nullptr` when absent, so every call site that uses the result would need changing. A takes the `Vec<FloorState>` directly, while B takes a `Session&` and reads `s.game.floors`, so the inputs differ too.

what_a: Returns the gold needed to advance from the membership's current level, calculated with that membership's guild gold factor (SRD R25).
what_b: Computes the gold needed to advance a character from their current level in a given guild, by summing a per-level cost that scales with the guild's gold factor and rounding the total to whole gold.
diff: Known: (1) B takes the guild factor from the table `kGuildGoldFactor[g]`, while A uses the membership's own `guildGold`, so they differ whenever those disagree. (2) B rounds the total half-even, and its comment flags that the community loop rounds half-up, so A differs wherever `goldForLevel` rounds differently or doesn't round. (3) B returns 0 for level <= 0, while A's result there depends on `goldForLevel`. Unverifiable: A's results for all inputs, since `goldForLevel`'s body is not shown.

what_a: Returns the name of the guild the character is currently active in, for display on the Look page row, or an empty string if the guild index is out of range.
what_b: Looks up the display name of a quest guild from a name table by its enum index, returning an empty string if the index is out of range.
diff: Both map a guild index to a name and return an empty string when the index is out of range, but they read different sources. A reads `s.data.guilds[g].name` with `g = c.activeGuild` and bounds `g` by `s.data.guilds.size()`. B reads `kQuestGuildNames[guild]` and bounds the index by `kGuildCount`. Results differ when (1) `s.data.guilds[g].name` differs from `kQuestGuildNames[g]` for an in-range `g`, (2) `g` is in `[kGuildCount, guilds.size())`, where A returns a name and B returns empty, or (3) `g` is in `[guilds.size(), kGuildCount)`, where A returns empty and B returns a name.

what_a: Maps a pen alignment index (0, 1, or 2) to its display name for the confinement pens: Good, Neutral, or Evil, with any value other than 0 or 1 treated as Evil.
what_b: Maps the Align enum (Good, Neutral, Evil) to its display string, returning "?" for any unrecognized value.
diff: For the valid values 0, 1, 2 (assuming Align::Good/Neutral/Evil have underlying values 0/1/2, which the pen-index comment implies but doesn't confirm), both return "Good", "Neutral", "Evil". They differ for integers outside 0..2: A returns "Evil" (e.g. -1, 3, 99), while B cannot receive such values as a typed Align, and an out-of-range Align cast from an int would hit B's "?" fallback.

what_a: Parses a string of up to six decimal digits into a non-negative integer without using exceptions, returning false if the string is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
what_b: Parses a non-negative decimal integer from a string without throwing exceptions, returning false for empty, non-numeric, or out-of-range (above 1,000,000) input.
diff: A rejects inputs longer than 6 characters, so "1000000" and "0000001" return false in A but may return true in B (B accepts up to 1000000 inclusive). A also rejects any non-digit character, so "+5", " 5", and "-0" return false in A, while B's result depends on accParseInt, which isn't shown and may accept them. Both reject empty and non-digit input in the common case.

what_a: Returns the spell point cost to cast a spell, which is zero when the cast comes from an item (itemLevel nonzero) and otherwise is the caster's spellbook cost from the spell cost engine.
what_b: Computes the spell point cost a party member would pay to cast a given spell with no item involved, returning false if the member or spell doesn't exist.
diff: With a valid member and spell and itemLevel 0, both return the same value (spellCostEngine). They differ when itemLevel is nonzero, where A returns 0 but B has no item-level parameter and always computes the full cost. They also differ when the member or spell doesn't exist, where B returns false and leaves `out` unset, while A takes references and has no such failure path. Their signatures differ too: A returns i32, while B takes a Session and indices, returns bool, and writes an i64 out-parameter.

what_a: Rounds a fractional value to the nearest whole number using round-half-even, implementing the game's B(.) rounding rule (with 30.77 rounding to 31 as the engine's preference).
what_b: Rounds a double to the nearest integer using round-half-to-even (banker's rounding) and returns it as an i64, with no game meaning of its own.
diff: Both round half to even and agree for all inputs with |x| < 2^31 after rounding, including negative halves (-2.5 gives -2, -3.5 gives -4). They differ for results outside the i32 range (|x| >= 2^31, e.g. 3e9), where A's static_cast<i32> truncates or is undefined while B returns the correct i64 value. For NaN and infinity, both are undefined behaviour in their casts, so neither gives a usable result.

what_a: Parses a string of 1 or 2 ASCII digits into a non-negative integer, returning false if the text is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
what_b: Parses a string of digits into a non-negative integer, rejecting empty strings, signs, non-digit characters, and values above 100000.
diff: A rejects any input longer than 2 characters, while B accepts any length as long as the value is at most 100000. So "100", "123", "99999", and "100000" give true in B and false in A. "007" gives false in A and true (value 7) in B. Both return false for "", signs, non-digits, and values above 100000, and both return the same value for inputs of 1 or 2 digits without leading zeros (e.g. "0", "42", "99").

what_a: Looks up a party member slot by a 1-based number or a case-insensitive character name, returning its 0-based index or -1 if no member matches.
what_b: Parses a 1-based party member number typed as a string, checks it falls within the party size, and converts it to a 0-based index.
diff: For numeric tokens in range, both return the same 0-based index. For name tokens (e.g. "Aragorn"), A returns the matching member's index but B returns false. For numeric tokens out of range, A returns -1 and B returns false. Inputs where parseInt and parseNum disagree (such as overflow) can't be determined from these excerpts.

what_a: Returns the string value stored under a given key in the session's feature-state map, or an empty string if the key is absent.
what_b: Looks up a string-valued key in a JSON object and returns its string value, or an empty string if the key is missing.
diff: Both return the stored string for a present key and an empty Str for an absent key. They differ when the stored value is not a JSON string: B returns `v->asString()` for any JSON value (numbers, booleans, objects, arrays, null), so its result depends on what `asString` returns for those types, which I could not see. A returns the stored value unchanged. Keys with embedded NULs also differ, because B takes a `const char*` and A takes a `Str`.

what_a: Charges a town cost to a party member, taking gold on hand first and then the bank, and first asks the CoverShortfall mod hook to cover any shortfall, refusing the charge with "Not enough gold!" if no cover applies.
what_b: Charges gold from the character's purse, taking from gold on hand first and then from the bank, and refuses the charge without taking anything if the purse can't cover the amount.
diff: (1) A clamps a negative cost to 0 and charges nothing, while B with a negative amount passes the checks and adds gold to goldOnHand; (2) when the purse is short and the CoverShortfall hook covers it, A charges and succeeds but B returns false; (3) with an out-of-range payerIndex, A returns unpaid while B has no index argument; (4) with a negative goldOnHand, A leaves goldOnHand unchanged and charges the full amount to the bank, while B zeroes goldOnHand and charges the remainder to the bank; (5) A calls ctx.say on refusal, B is silent, and A returns a ChargeResult where B returns a bool.

what_a: Builds the featureState lookup key string "hall.<k>.<field>" from a record index and field name, with no game rule applied.
what_b: Builds a namespaced string key ("raise.<member>.<field>") from a party member number and a field name, with no game meaning of its own.
diff: Every input differs. The literal prefix is "hall." in hallKey and "raise." in raiseKey, so hallKey(3, "x") returns "hall.3.x" and raiseKey(3, "x") returns "raise.3.x". Otherwise both build "<prefix><integer>.<field>" the same way.

what_a: Parses a string as a signed 64-bit decimal integer, rejecting any non-digit characters or overflow, and writes the result to the output parameter.
what_b: Parses a string into a signed 64-bit integer, accepting an optional leading minus sign and rejecting non-digit characters or values above 10^12.
diff: Both reject empty strings, a lone "-", non-digit characters, and "+" signs, and both accept leading zeros and "-0". They differ in the magnitude limit: B rejects any value above 1000000000000 (and below -1000000000000), while A accepts up to the i64 maximum 9223372036854775807. For example, "1000000000001" gives true from A and false from B, and "9223372036854775807" gives true from A and false from B. Values from 1000000000001 through 9223372036854775807 (and their negatives) are the only inputs where the results differ.

what_a: Formats a signed 1/10000-gold amount as a human-readable string with up to four decimal places and trailing zeros removed, followed by " gold".
what_b: Formats a signed 1/10000-gold currency amount as a decimal gold string with a minus sign for negatives and four fractional digits zero-padded.
diff: Both convert 1/10000-gold units to a signed decimal string, but they differ for every input with a non-zero value. A appends " gold" and B does not. A drops trailing zeros and the decimal point when the fraction is zero, while B always prints four decimal places. Examples: 0 gives "0 gold" (A) vs "0.0000" (B); 120000 gives "12 gold" vs "12.0000"; 5000 gives "0.5 gold" vs "0.5000"; 12345 gives "1.2345 gold" vs "1.2345"; -5000 gives "-0.5 gold" vs "-0.5000".

what_a: Searches a list of floor states for the one whose dungeon level matches the given level and returns its index, or -1 if none matches.
what_b: Looks up the stored floor whose dungeon level matches the party's current dungeon level, returning nullptr if no such floor is saved.
diff: Both find the first floor whose dungeonLevel matches. A takes the level as an argument and returns its index (or -1 if none); B reads the level from s.game.party.dungeonLevel and returns a pointer to the floor (or nullptr if none). So for the same floors and level, A's index i corresponds to B's &floors[i], and A's -1 corresponds to B's nullptr. Call sites would need changes beyond argument form, since the return type and the source of the level both differ.

what_a: Returns a reference to the square at grid coordinates (x, y) in the floor's square array, by converting the coordinates to a cell index.
what_b: Returns a pointer to the square at 1-based coordinates (x, y) in a floor's row-major square array, or nullptr if the coordinates fall outside the 30-wide map or past the end of the stored squares.
diff: Out-of-range inputs differ: B returns nullptr for x < 1, y < 1, x > 30, or an index at or past squares.size(), while A computes cellOf(x, y) and indexes unchecked, which is undefined behaviour or a wrong square. Returning a non-const reference (A) versus a const pointer (B) also means call sites that check for nullptr can't take A without changing code beyond argument form. For in-range inputs the results match only if cellOf(x, y) equals (x - 1) + 30 * (y - 1), which I could not verify because cellOf's definition wasn't provided.

what_a: Parses a text string into a 1-based party member number and returns false if the text isn't a number or falls outside the valid party size range.
what_b: Parses a party member number from the second word of a typed command and checks that it falls within the current party size, returning whether it is valid.
diff: The upper bound differs. A accepts 1..kPartyMaxSize (a fixed constant), while B accepts 1..accPartySize(s) (the session's current party size). For example, with a party of 2 and kPartyMaxSize of 4, input "3" is accepted by A and rejected by B. Their inputs also differ: A takes the already-extracted text, while B takes a token vector and returns false when it has fewer than 2 entries. Parsing may differ too, since companionsParseNumber and accParseInt are not shown, so inputs such as "+2", " 2", or "2x" may be handled differently.

what_a: Rolls a percentile die (one random draw) against a hit threshold, returning true if the attack passes the gate, per the Mordor melee hit rule R18 (miss when roll reaches the threshold).
what_b: Rolls a percentile die (1–100) against the monster's computed hit chance, returning true if the monster's attack hits the character.
diff: Both use a uniform roll in 1..100, but A passes when roll < threshold and B passes when roll <= chance. For integer values, A(threshold=t) matches B(chance=t-1) exactly, so they differ at every integer value: at 50, A passes 49 rolls (49%) and B passes 50 (50%). For fractional chance, no integer threshold reproduces B: at 5.4, B passes rolls 1-5 (five values), while A passes four at threshold 5 and five at threshold 6. Chance below 1 (e.g. 0.5) passes nothing in B, which matches A only at threshold 0 or lower. A also draws via ctx.rng.nextDouble() and B via ctx.rng.below(100), so even with identical distributions, the same seed may produce different outcomes (not verified from the code shown).

what_a: Parses a string of digits into a non-negative integer, rejecting empty strings, signs, non-digit characters, and values above 100000.
what_b: Parses a string into a signed 64-bit integer, accepting an optional leading minus sign and rejecting non-digit characters or values above 10^12.
diff: Negative inputs: "-5" (and "-0", "-100000") are rejected by A but accepted by B (giving -5, 0, -100000). Values above 100000 up to 1000000000000: "100001" and "999999" are rejected by A but accepted by B. Values above 1000000000000 (e.g. "1000000000001") are rejected by both. A returns i32 and B returns i64, so B can represent results A cannot, though this only matters for inputs already listed. Empty input and "-" alone are rejected by both, and all inputs in 0..100000 give identical results.

what_a: Looks up a stored record field (for a given kind and name, such as a monster or item entry) in the session's feature state and returns its string value, or an empty string if it is absent.
what_b: Looks up a string value by key in the session's feature-state map and returns it, or a supplied default if the key is absent.
diff: When the key is absent from `s.featureState`, A returns an empty string while B returns `dflt`, so they differ for any call where `dflt` is non-empty. A also builds its key as `kRecordPrefix + kind + "." + name + "." + field`, while B uses `key` verbatim, so they look up different entries for the same arguments. Results match only when `dflt` is empty and the key equals A's composed key. Found entries always return the stored value in both.

what_a: Parses a string of 1 to 4 digits into a non-negative integer, returning false if any character is not a decimal digit.
what_b: Parses a string of decimal digits into a 32-bit integer, rejecting empty input, non-digit characters, and values above 1,000,000.
diff: They accept different inputs with length or magnitude above 4 digits. A rejects any input longer than 4 characters, so "10000", "12345", "1000000", and "00001" return false. B accepts those (values 10000, 12345, 1000000, and 1) because it only caps the numeric value at 1000000 inclusive, so "1000001" and larger are rejected by B and A alike. Both accept "9999" and reject "", "-5", and "12a". A's range is 0 to 9999; B's is 0 to 1000000.

what_a: Parses a string of up to six decimal digits into a non-negative integer without using exceptions, returning false if the string is empty, too long, or contains any non-digit character.
what_b: Parses a string of digits into a non-negative integer, rejecting empty strings, signs, non-digit characters, and values above 100000.
diff: A accepts 100001 through 999999 (e.g. "100001", "999999") and B rejects them, since B caps values at 100000. B accepts zero-padded words longer than 6 characters (e.g. "0000001" gives 1), and A rejects them because of its length check of 6. Both accept "100000" and "0", and both reject "", "+5", "-5", and any non-digit.

what_a: Parses a text string into a 1-based companion slot number, returning false if the text isn't a number or falls outside 1 to kCompanionSlots.
what_b: Parses a string of digits into an integer party slot number between 1 and kPartyMaxSize, returning -1 if the text is not a valid slot.
diff: Inputs with 3+ characters such as "001" or "010" are rejected by parseMember (returns -1) but may be accepted by companionsParseSlot, depending on companionsParseNumber, which isn't shown. Signed or padded text such as "+1" or " 1" is also a possible difference, since parseMember accepts digits only. If kCompanionSlots and kPartyMaxSize differ, valid upper bounds differ too. Return conventions differ: companionsParseSlot returns bool and writes slot1, while parseMember returns the slot or -1, so call sites need more than an argument-form change.

what_a: Linear search over the game's floor list that returns a pointer to the floor whose dungeon level matches the given level, or null if none does.
what_b: Looks up the stored floor whose dungeon level matches the party's current dungeon level, returning nullptr if no such floor is saved.
diff: For any `level` equal to `s.game.party.dungeonLevel`, both return the same floor pointer (first match, or nullptr). They differ when `level` is any other value: A finds that floor, while B can only search the party's level. B also returns `const FloorState*` and takes `const Session&`, whereas A returns a mutable `FloorState*` and takes `Session&`, so A cannot replace B where a const pointer or const session is required, and B cannot replace A where mutation through the result is needed.

what_a: Decides whether a guild accepts a character of a given race by checking the guild's race bitmask, treating out-of-range race indices as allowed.
what_b: Looks up in the race-guild eligibility grid (T4) whether a given race is allowed to join a given guild, returning that yes/no answer.
diff: Both encode race-guild eligibility, but they read different data. A tests `guildDef.raceMask` bit `raceIndex`, while B looks up `kGuildGrid[raceIndex(race)][guild]`. A returns true for any negative index or any index >= kRaceRecordCount, whereas B has no such guard and indexes the grid out of bounds (undefined behaviour). For in-range inputs the results agree only if each guild's raceMask matches its grid column, which I could not verify from these two excerpts.

what_a: Parses a string of decimal digits into a 32-bit integer, rejecting empty input, non-digit characters, and values above 1,000,000.
what_b: Parses a string into a signed 64-bit integer, accepting an optional leading minus sign and rejecting non-digit characters or values above 10^12.
diff: B accepts a leading '-' and A rejects it (e.g. "-5" gives -5 in B, false in A; "-0" gives 0 in B, false in A). A accepts only 0 to 1000000 and B accepts 0 to 1000000000000, so "1000001" through "1000000000000" (and negatives in that range) succeed only in B. Both reject "", "-", "+5", non-digit text, and values above their own limits. Within A's accepted non-negative range the two agree, and A's output is i32 where B's is i64.

what_a: Returns the spell point cost to cast a spell, which is zero when the cast comes from an item (itemLevel nonzero) and otherwise is the caster's spellbook cost from the spell cost engine.
what_b: Computes the spell-point cost of casting a given spell for the caster by checking each guild the caster belongs to that can reach the spell, pricing it with the guild's spell rate and the caster's guild spell level, and keeping the cheapest accepted price (raised to the smallest rated level seen), or 0 if no guild can cast it.
diff: For itemLevel == 0, A returns exactly what B returns, so B(ctx, caster, spell) is A(ctx, caster, spell, 0). For itemLevel != 0, A returns 0 while B returns its guild-based price, e.g. any caster with a qualifying guild and spell where B is nonzero.

what_a: Parses a decimal integer string (with optional leading minus sign) into a 64-bit value, setting an ok flag to false if any character is not a digit.
what_b: Parses a string of decimal digits with an optional leading minus sign into a 32-bit integer, returning false if the text is malformed or the magnitude exceeds 1,000,000,000.
diff: A accepts magnitudes above 1000000000 and B rejects them, e.g. "1000000001", "-1000000001", "2147483647", "9999999999" (A returns ok=true with the value; B returns false). A accepts up to the i64 range (and overflows undefinedly past 19 digits), while B caps at ±1000000000 inclusive. On failure, A sets the return value to 0 and ok=false, while B returns false and leaves `out` unmodified. Both agree on "", "-", "+5", " 5", "12a" (reject) and "-0" and "1000000000" (accept, giving 0 and 1000000000).

what_a: Linear search over the loaded floor definitions that returns a pointer to the floor whose levelNum matches the given dungeon level, or null if none does.
what_b: Scans the game's floor table for the entry whose level number matches the requested level and returns a pointer to it, or null if none exists.
diff: Only when `data.floors.size()` exceeds 2^32-1. Function A's `u32` index wraps, so matches at positions >= 2^32 are never checked and it returns nullptr where B returns a pointer. This requires billions of floor entries, so it is unreachable in practice.

what_a: Case-insensitively matches a typed word against the quest guild names and, on a hit, sets the guild output to the matching enum value and returns true, otherwise returning false.
what_b: Parses a typed word as either a numeric index or a case-insensitive name into a Guild enum value, returning false if neither matches a valid guild.
diff: (1) Numeric input: B accepts a string that parses as an integer in 0..kGuildCount-1 (e.g. "2") and returns that guild, while A returns false. (2) Name table: A matches against kQuestGuildNames and B against kGuildNames, so any name present in one table but not the other is accepted by only one function. (3) Normalization: A applies accLower to both sides, while B lowers only the input and compares it to the raw kGuildNames entries, so an input differing only in accents or case can match in A but not B (or the reverse, depending on how accLower and lowered treat accents).

what_a: Parses a decimal integer string (with optional leading minus sign) into a 64-bit value, setting an ok flag to false if any character is not a digit.
what_b: Parses a string of 1 to 4 digits into a non-negative integer, returning false if any character is not a decimal digit.
diff: Negative input: "-5" gives ok=true, value -5 in A, but false in B. Length: "12345" and "00001" give ok=true in A but false in B (B accepts at most 4 characters). Failure output: on failure A returns 0 and sets ok=false, while B leaves `out` unchanged. Overflow: A has no bounds check and overflows i64 on very long digit strings, while B cannot overflow. Both reject "", "-", and "+5" (A never accepts a leading '+').

what_a: Looks up the character's best guild rating (attack and defence values) and returns them as an (att, def) pair, which the combat and total-AD rules use as input.
what_b: Computes a character's best guild attack and defense bonuses by taking the maximum att and def values across all guilds the character has joined.
diff: The only difference is the return type: bestGuildPair returns AdPair and bestGuildAD returns BestAd. For every Character, the att and def values are identical, because bestGuildPair just copies bestGuildAD's fields. Swapping them at call sites therefore needs changes to how the result is used, not just to the arguments.

what_a: Returns a reference to the square at grid coordinates (x, y) in the floor's square array, by converting the coordinates to a cell index.
what_b: Looks up the square at the given x, y coordinates on a dungeon floor, using the floor's width from the game data (or a default width), and returns a pointer to it or null if the level or coordinates are invalid.
diff: For in-range coordinates on a floor whose width matches what `cellOf` uses, both return the same square. They differ when: (a) x or y is out of range, where B returns nullptr but A indexes out of bounds (undefined behaviour); (b) level < 1 or no floor has that dungeonLevel, where B returns nullptr and A has no such check; (c) the floor's width differs from the one `cellOf` uses, where the results differ, though `cellOf` is not shown, so this is unverified; (d) A returns a reference and B a pointer, so call sites need adjusting.

what_a: Looks up a string value by key in the session's feature-state map and returns it, or a supplied default if the key is absent.
what_b: Looks up a string-valued key in a JSON object and returns its string value, or an empty string if the key is missing.
diff: (1) Key absent: A returns the caller's `dflt`, while B always returns an empty string, so they differ whenever `dflt` is non-empty. (2) Key present with a non-string JSON value (number, bool, null, object, array): A returns the stored `Str` unchanged, while B returns `v->asString()`, which may produce a different string or an empty one depending on how `asString` handles non-string types. (3) Argument forms differ (Session and Str key versus JsonValue and const char* key), which is permitted by the question.

what_a: Searches a list of floor states for the one whose dungeon level matches the given level and returns its index, or -1 if none matches.
what_b: Scans the game's floor table for the entry whose level number matches the requested level and returns a pointer to it, or null if none exists.
diff: A searches `floors` (FloorState, field `dungeonLevel`) and returns the index of the first match as `i32`, or `-1` if none. B searches `data.floors` (FloorDef, field `levelNum`) and returns a pointer to the first match, or `nullptr` if none. Any call site must change its argument (vector vs. GameData) and its return handling (index/-1 vs. pointer/nullptr), and the two functions give different answers if the FloorState list and the static FloorDef list disagree about which levels exist.

what_a: Resolves one monster melee blow against the target, computing the damage the monster deals from its strength, level, and damage modifier (using a placeholder archive damage formula, since the real blow body isn't in the sources).
what_b: Computes the base melee damage a monster deals to a character each round, scaled by the monster's strength and guild level and reduced by the character's defence against the monster's attack, with a random roll.
diff: For every input where B's result fits in i32, A returns the same value and consumes the same RNG draws. A differs only when B's result exceeds INT32_MAX: A's `static_cast<i32>` then overflows (undefined behaviour in C++), while B returns the full value as f64. A's return type is also i32 rather than f64.

what_a: Returns a copy of the given string with every character converted to lowercase, which is used for case-insensitive INI key matching and has no game meaning.
what_b: Returns a copy of the input string with all ASCII uppercase letters converted to lowercase.
diff: Under the default "C" locale the two agree on every input. If the program calls setlocale() with a Latin-1-style locale, A also lowercases bytes 0xC0-0xDE (e.g. 0xC0 becomes 0xE0) while B leaves them unchanged, so the results differ for those non-ASCII bytes.

what_a: Parses a string of decimal digits into a 32-bit integer, rejecting empty input, non-digit characters, and values above 1,000,000.
what_b: Parses a string as a signed 64-bit decimal integer, rejecting any non-digit characters or overflow, and writes the result to the output parameter.
diff: Both reject empty strings, "+5", "-" alone, and any non-digit characters, and both leave `out` untouched on failure. They differ on: "-5" and other negative values (A rejects, B accepts); "1000001" through "9223372036854775807" (A rejects because it caps at 1000000, B accepts); "-9223372036854775808" (B rejects, since its accumulator can't reach 2^63); and the output type (A writes i32, B writes i64, so B can return values that A can't represent).

what_a: Looks up the square at the given x, y coordinates on a dungeon floor, using the floor's width from the game data (or a default width), and returns a pointer to it or null if the level or coordinates are invalid.
what_b: Converts 1-based (x, y) grid coordinates into an index in the flat square array of a floor, returning a pointer to that square or nullptr if the coordinates or index fall outside the map.
diff: (1) Level < 1: A returns nullptr; B has no level argument. (2) Width: A uses the floor's width from `s.data.floors`, or `kRescueDefaultWidth` if no definition exists; B always uses `kMapWidth`. They differ whenever those widths differ. (3) x > width: A doesn't check this, so x = width+1 wraps to x = 1 of the next row; B returns nullptr for x > kMapWidth. (4) x < 1: A wraps to the previous row when y ≥ 2 (e.g. x=0, y=2 returns the square at (width, 1)); B returns nullptr. (5) y < 1: A can return a square when x > width (e.g. x=width+1, y=0 returns (1,1)); B returns nullptr. (6) A returns nullptr when no floor matches `level`, which B has no equivalent for.

what_a: Formats a gold amount stored in 1/10000 gold units as a decimal string with a " gold" suffix, omitting the fractional part when it is zero.
what_b: Formats a signed 1/10000-gold amount as a human-readable string with up to four decimal places and trailing zeros removed, followed by " gold".
diff: (1) Trailing zeros in the fraction: A always prints four fraction digits, B drops trailing zeros. For units=5000, A gives "0.5000 gold" and B gives "0.5 gold". For units=10001 both give "1.0001 gold". (2) Negative units: A has no sign handling. For units=-5000 it gives whole=0 and emits non-digit characters from the negative remainder (e.g. '+'); for units=-15000 it gives a malformed string. B gives "-0.5 gold" and "-1.5 gold". Non-negative inputs with zero fraction (e.g. 10000 → "1 gold") and non-negative inputs with fractions that have no trailing zeros (e.g. 10001) match.

what_a: Parses a string of 1 to 4 digits into a non-negative integer, returning false if any character is not a decimal digit.
what_b: Parses a string as a signed 64-bit decimal integer, rejecting any non-digit characters or overflow, and writes the result to the output parameter.
diff: (1) Leading '-': B accepts "-5" (out = -5) and "-0" (out = 0); A returns false for both. (2) Length: A returns false for any input longer than 4 characters, so "00001" and "10000" are rejected; B accepts them ("00001" gives 1, "10000" gives 10000). (3) Range: A caps at 9999; B accepts up to kI64Max (and down to -kI64Max). (4) Output type: A writes an i32, B an i64, so call sites must change their variable type as well as their argument form. Both reject "", "-", and any non-digit characters, and both accept "0", "1234", and "0042" with the same value.

what_a: Converts a double into a fixed-point Currency value by scaling by the currency unit and rounding half to even, returning 0 if the result would overflow the range.
what_b: Rounds a double to four decimal places using half-even rounding and returns it as a 64-bit fixed-point integer, with no game meaning of its own.
diff: Inputs where `d * 10000` is at or beyond ±9.2e18, including values in (9.2e18, ~9.22e18] that still fit in i64, and infinities and NaN. For these, A returns 0 while B passes the value to `roundHalfEven`, which gives an out-of-range or undefined result (for example, `d = 1e15`). This assumes `kCurrencyUnit` is 10000 and both use the same `roundHalfEven`, neither of which is shown.

what_a: Parses a text string into a 1-based party member number and returns false if the text isn't a number or falls outside the valid party size range.
what_b: Parses a string of digits into an integer party slot number between 1 and kPartyMaxSize, returning -1 if the text is not a valid slot.
diff: Both accept exactly the slot numbers 1..kPartyMaxSize written as plain decimal digits (e.g. "1", "12"), but they differ on other inputs. B rejects any string longer than 2 characters, so "001" returns -1, while A accepts it if companionsParseNumber accepts leading zeros. A's handling of "+1", " 1", "-0", and "" depends on companionsParseNumber, which isn't shown, so I can't confirm those agree with B. Also, B signals failure with -1 and A with false plus an out-parameter, so call sites need a form change.

what_a: If the actor's aimed monster group has no standing monsters left, retargets the actor to the first group that still has standing monsters (rule R15).
what_b: Implements R3 of the melee rules: further swings stay on the aimed group while it still has standing members, and otherwise aim shifts to the first standing group.
diff: When the aimed group is not standing and no group is standing, A leaves `actor.order.aimedGroup` unchanged, while B returns `firstStandingGroup(enc)`, which may be -1 or another sentinel (its body is unknown). A also writes the result into the actor, while B returns it, which changes call-site form but not the rule. Whether B matches A elsewhere depends on the unseen `aimMustMove` and `firstStandingGroup` bodies, which I assumed correspond to `!groupStanding` and `standingGroupIndex(ctx, game, -1)`.

what_a: Compares two strings for equality ignoring trailing spaces and letter case, a generic text helper that the roster name matching uses.
what_b: Compares two strings for exact equality by checking that their lengths match and that one starts with the other.
diff: A ignores trailing spaces and ASCII case, so sameName("Bob", "bob") and sameName("Bob ", "Bob") return true, while seerSameText returns false for both (if seerStartsWith is a plain case-sensitive prefix test, B is exact equality). Both return true for identical strings, and both return false when lengths differ after A's trailing-space trim. A trims only ' ', not tabs. Behaviour of seerStartsWith was not provided and is assumed here.

what_a: Returns a reference to the item's definition by indexing the game's item table directly with the item's id, with no game rule applied.
what_b: Looks up an item's definition record from the game's item table by its id, returning a pointer to it or null when the id is negative or out of range.
diff: For in-range ids (0 <= id < items.size()) both return the same element. For id < 0, A converts the id to u32 and indexes out of bounds (undefined behaviour), while B returns nullptr. For id >= items.size(), A indexes out of bounds (undefined behaviour), while B returns nullptr. A returns `const ItemDef&` and B returns `const ItemDef*`, so call sites that bind or dereference the result differently will not compile without changes.
